en: Had not the smallest hole anywhere;
Its fastenings numbered nine,
And he buttoned it and made ready,
Buckled his sword in its sheath,
And prepared all his weapons—
Ready to die if true death came,
Ready to challenge
Brave Kyyaz of the Jediger,
To grapple with him,
And clash thunderously in battle,
Ready to die if fate decreed,
And make the vile swine Kyyaz
Suffer torment at his hands.
“If my strength fails and proves too little,
If I falter and retreat from the clash,
May I endure misery unknown among men;
And if I do not die
At the hands of Kyyaz of the Jediger,
May I early behold at the infidel’s hands
The narrow road from which none return.
But if my strength rises and proves enough,
May I throw mighty Kyyaz
Flat upon his back,
Drag him along the road,
And proclaim it to the Dangyt people;
May I scoop up and drink my fill
Of the black blood within his heart,
And only then cast aside
The anguished misery of my humiliation.
When I fight Kyyaz,
May I lay him flat upon his back.
He loudly seized booty,
And slaughtered my strongest men;
He butchered all our heroes,
And cut down so many
Of our tender young warriors.
He crushed our gray wolves,
And spilled the blood of many people;
He slew my falcon outright,
And took every southern woman,
Old and young, as plunder.
He plundered my migrating people,
Binding us together with ropes,
Thrusting spears with deadly aim,
Firing guns and drawing bows,
And fighting in a roaring tumult;
He scattered my caravan across the open plain.
From dragon-like Kyyaz,
By the power of Father God,
I mean to take my revenge.
Ah, accursed Kyyaz,
Once I have traced your lineage,
From that vicious dog himself—
At the hollow of Kashatchy,
On Khan Kyyaz’s road,
Beside the new irrigation ditch,
By the echoing cliff,
At the narrow pass for a single horse,
At the junction of nine roads,
Where wolves tear the carcasses of sheep,
On the shoulder where the mountains end,
At the place where Kyyaz would come,
Külchoro, guarded by the spirits,
Lay with a white stone for his pillow,
His head turned toward the qibla,
Wrapped in his bulletproof armor,
His weapons prepared.
His outstretched leg did not draw back,
His closed eyes did not open,
His snoring did not cease;
He slept soundly, utterly unconcerned,
Regarding mighty Kyyaz’s coming
As worth no more than the hem of his robe.
Courage and lionhearted valor
Had been granted beyond measure
To Choro, guarded by the spirits.
Though lion-born brave Kyyaz
Was riding down upon him,
He valued him less than the hem of his robe.
Courage and proud daring
The Almighty Lord
Had bestowed without measure
Upon the lion and gray wolf Choro.
He did not think Kyyaz of the Jediger
Was any mighty lion;
He gave no thought to death,
Counted true peril as nothing,
And did not spare his tiny life:
“May I bring utter grief
Upon brave Kyyaz;
Though I have been plundered and crushed,
May I fight tirelessly for six months
And somehow avenge my wrongs.
Now I shall avenge that ancient wrong.
Brave Kyyaz’s humiliation of me,
His tyranny, never leaves my mind.
He slaughtered my ruined people
And cut away the sinew
From behind my right shoulder.
I had no remedy and no strength;
I lived long as a slave in this foul world.
My heart burned, my liver was aflame,
But my orphan has come, and I have matured.
My pent-up grief has opened to speech,
The shame exposed behind me is covered,
And my honor has now been restored.
My torn seams have been mended,
My valiant Seytek has grown,
The pain of my sickness has eased,
And my eyes, sealed as with paste, have opened.
Now it is my turn to raise
A towering pavilion on the open plain.
It is my turn to take revenge on my tormentor,
My turn to become a hero.
In the narrow defile of the open country,
It is time to recover my caravan.
In that dragon’s narrow pass,
It is time to take revenge.
My ribs have grown firm,
And compared with former days,
The flesh around my ankles has filled out.
Against Kyyaz of the Jediger,
We shall break each other’s ribs,
And spill blood like hail.
Against the infidel in his full strength,
Against bloodthirsty warrior Kyyaz,
I am going to test myself in combat,
To grapple and die;
I am going forth to my death.
I am setting out to behold
The narrow road from which none return.”
So spoke brave Choro.
Choro, sound in all twelve limbs, said:
“How shall I take my revenge
If I do not turn and strike his flank,
If I do not bring down the villain first,
If I do not unleash turmoil
Over the sixty young wives and widows
He carried away as plunder?
After so much death and humiliation,
If I do not avenge myself anew,
May I sink away as though never born;
May I die rather than live.
I shall confront Kyyaz
And break his ribs.
I shall heap humiliation on him like sheep;
We shall ram and fight,
Enduring disgrace,
Seizing and tearing at each other’s ears,
Wrenching and straining against each other,
Cutting off heads like those of sheep,
Ripping bellies open like melons,
Ramming and battling,
Standing locked in desperate strife,
Fighting with our lives cast aside;
I shall bring a dreadful calamity upon him.
From boastful Kyyaz
I shall take my old revenge.
While my mighty head still lives,
He plundered my people
And broke my waist across,
Extinguishing like a dying fire
The spirit I had cherished,
Leaving me weeping in humiliation and grief,
Driven from my encamped people.
While my round head still lives,
How can I surrender my people?
With frenzied warrior Kyyaz
I shall fight to the full,
And test myself in the struggle.
I shall aim and thrust my spear;
From fierce warrior Kyyaz,
From the infidel who ravaged the people,
The earth itself shook and turned.
Bölökbay, the consummate craftsman,
Who had befriended the prophet David,
Took up a file and worked the iron.
Over a treasure beyond comprehension,
He and David took counsel.
He fashioned the battle-axe,
Perfecting every curve;
Its socket was steel and its edge was sharp.
So that it would never recoil from the foe,
He laid steel along its blade,
And David bent and tempered it to perfection.
“So Choro may be its master,”
He had a holy elder bless it.
While he was making it,
The strain upon his forge was so great
That tribute fell upon the Kyrgyz,
And many young bulls were slaughtered.
The strain upon his forge was so great
That a blue bend of forest was felled.
He hammered out its keen edge,
So whatever it struck would not survive,
But die doubled over,
Its appointed doom fully met,
Yellowing for want of any cure,
And swiftly departing this world;
He quenched it in human tears.
He made every piece of equipment ready
And buckled on his battle-axe.
Fate’s line had now been drawn:
Brave Kyyaz was destined to meet
Fortunate brave Choro.
At a spur of the shouldered mountain,
At the tip of the Sekichek ridge,
His strength and courage
Had now surpassed all others.
He had lain in wait for brave Kyyaz
Of the Jediger, saying,
“This is the path a hero must take.”
He would fight and test his strength,
His fame reaching distant Alay,
His name known throughout many lands.
Great and wise fierce hero,
Your battle cry stirred an uproar;
Your courage and lionheartedness
Surpassed those of all other mortals.
To bar valiant Kyyaz’s road,
He summoned all his courage,
Ready to die if death arrived,
And, if fortune allowed, to make
A spectacle of Kyyaz.
His threadlike life turned to ash,
His mind surged into frenzy;
He gave no thought to dying
And did not spare his life from death.
Lion Choro, guarded by the spirits,
Embarked upon a terrible feat of courage.
His precious, sweet life
He bound to a hair and cast away.
The golden-cheeked battle-axe—
Such was the nature of that axe:
Its span-long blade gaped broad,
Spreading blood wherever it struck;
Its crown was like a mace-sized fist—
Such was the nature of that weapon.
If you ask about the battle-axe,
It would not rebound even from stone;
If it struck iron in fury,
It would not spin back.
When swung straight at the foe,
Its blade flamed red with fire.
When its handle was grasped and swung,
Its shaft lengthened forty fathoms.
Set upon grass, it started a fire;
Whatever it struck died instantly.
When it struck stone, sparks flew,
And fragments burst like bullets;
It crushed whatever it bit into.
The lame smith Bölökbay
And great master David had forged it.
Will he slaughter every living soul?
Will he seize and devour my child?
